paper_title: Semantic Concept Steering Breaks the Explanation Drift Loop in Continual Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Catastrophic forgetting in continual learning (CL) manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as \emph{explanation drift}: models maintain predictive accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features to spurious correlations. This work identifies and resolves a previously overlooked structural flaw in explanation-aware CL: pixel-level saliency regularization derives supervision targets from the model's own frozen saliency maps, creating a \emph{self-referential drift loop} that actively reinforces spurious attention across tasks. We introduce \textbf{C$^3$L} (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning), which breaks this loop by anchoring regularization to class-consistent semantic concepts (e.g., ``curved beak'', ``striped pattern'') discovered offline, independent of model state, providing (i) target independence from model drift, and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency across every instance of a class. We identify that our concept-based objective, combined with approximate LRP relevance conservation, induces a \emph{crowding-out effect}: since concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction, enforcing high relevance within concept regions implicitly suppresses spurious background correlations without explicit penalization. \method does not require human-annotated concept sets, as it employs a fully automated concept discovery and spatial grounding. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks and over 20 baselines demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in accuracy, forgetting, explanation quality, spurious correlation mitigation, and out-of-distribution robustness.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Deep neural networks trained on static datasets catastrophically forget previously learned knowledge when adapted to sequential tasks [1, 2]. This phenomenon poses fundamental challenges for deploying adaptive systems in dynamic environments, from medical diagnosis systems learning new diseases to autonomous vehicles adapting to novel scenarios [3]. While the continual learning literature has developed sophisticated mechanisms to preserve predictive accuracy through replay [4, 5], regularization [6, 7], and architectural adaptations [8, 9], these approaches treat models as black boxes operating in parameter or feature space - preserving what is predicted, not how. The explanation drift problem. Ebrahimi et al. [10] showed that catastrophic forgetting manifests not only as accuracy degradation but also as explanation drift: models maintain accuracy while silently shifting attention from diagnostic features (e.g., bird beak shapes) to spurious correlations (e.g., background foliage). This instability in reasoning is not captured by standard metrics, yet has critical implications - when such spurious correlations fail under distribution shift, performance can collapse [11, 12]. Existing explanation-aware CL methods address this drift by regularizing pixel-level saliency maps [10, 13, 14], but they share fundamental and previously overlooked structural flaw: Pixel-level methods derive supervision targets from the models own frozen saliency at buffer insertion. If the model has already drifted toward spurious features at that point, these patterns become the regularization target, effectively reinforcing the drift across future tasks. This self-referential drift loop is not merely an attribution noise issue - it is structural property of any scheme that derives targets from model-state-dependent saliency. Breaking the loop with semantic concept anchoring. We present C3L (Concept-Consistent Continual Learning) (Figure 2), which breaks this loop by grounding regularization in class-consistent semantic concepts - human-interpretable visual attributes (e.g., curved beak) discovered offline, prior to and independent of any model state. This yields two structural properties no previous explanation-aware method can provide: (i) target independence - concept targets cannot encode model drift as they are produced independently of the learners state; and (ii) cross-instance semantic consistency - every instance of class is regularized toward the same diagnostic attributes, inducing class-level invariant beyond instance-specific saliency supervision. Figure 2: C3L Overview. Discriminative visual concepts are discovered offline via an LLM and spatially grounded using SAM 3, producing model-state-independent supervision targets that break the self-referential drift loop of prior pixel-level methods. During continual training, Lconcept anchors relevance to semantic regions via crowding-out effect, while Lstab preserves background spatial structure against task-specific drift. Furthermore, we identify crowding-out effect: under approximate LRP relevance conservation, concept and background regions compete for the relevance of the same prediction. Enforcing high 2 relevance within semantically grounded concept regions therefore implicitly suppresses spurious background attributions, without any explicit penalization, turning semantic anchoring into an implicit suppression mechanism, which we validate empirically. complementary background stability term preserves the spatial structure of background relevance while allowing its magnitude to shrink, preventing freed relevance mass from drifting toward new task-specific artifacts rather than toward diagnostic concepts. Finally, fully automated framework, leveraging LLMs for concept discovery [15] and open-vocabulary segmentation for spatial grounding [16], eliminates the manual annotation burden that has historically prevented concept-based approaches [17] from scaling to the many-class, sequential-task regime. Contributions: 1. Problem identification: We formalize the self-referential drift loop as structural obstacle in pixel-level explanation-aware CL (Section 3). 2. Crowding-out mechanism: We identify the crowding-out effect induced by approximate LRP conservation, which turns semantic anchoring into an implicit background-suppression mechanism, and validate it quantitatively. 3. C3L framework: novel concept-guided continual learning framework. It operates without manual annotation and leverages semantic anchors to eliminate self-referential drift and drive the generalization of transferable concepts in the model (4.5). 4. State-of-the-art results: C3L outperforms more than twenty baselines across five benchmarks on accuracy, forgetting, semantic localization, spurious correlation mitigation, and OOD robustness, on both CNN and ViT architectures.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Continual learning strategies. CL methods can be roughly divided into several types. Replay-based methods [4, 5, 18, 19] store exemplars and interleave them during new task training. Wan et al. [20] show that replay is essential for maintaining feature learning dynamics across tasks. Regularizationbased methods [6, 7, 21] add parameter regularization terms or function regularization terms to transfer knowledge from the old model to the new one. Architecture-based methods often add new trainable modules to expand the feature space for new tasks. Prompt-based [9, 22, 23] methods keep the backbone frozen and learn task-specific input prompts. Adapter-based methods [2427] insert learnable modules or selectively fine-tune components while freezing pretrained weights. Other approaches exploit frozen pretrained features through slow classifier learning or random projections [28, 29]. All these operate in parameter, feature, or sample space without preserving semantic reasoning - which visual features the model attends to. This leaves models vulnerable to explanation drift [10]. Explainable AI and saliency maps. Explainability methods aim to reveal which input features drive models prediction. Model-agnostic approaches such as LIME [30] and SHAP [31], as well as learned explainers [32], apply across domains, and dedicated attribution techniques have been developed for recommender systems [3337] and for language models [3841]. In computer vision, explanations are typically given as saliency maps, produced by gradient-based methods such as Grad-CAM [42] and its extensions to similarity models [43] and transformers [44]; by relevance-propagation methods that approximately conserve relevance, such as LRP [45, 46] and AttnLRP [47]; and by path-integration methods originating from Integrated Gradients [48], later extended to integration over intermediate representations [49, 50], stochastic and probabilistic paths and baselines [51, 52], and metric-adapted baselines [53]. Related work revisits the completeness property underlying conservation-based attribution [54] and the human-aligned evaluation of saliency maps [55]. Concept-based explanations link attributions to human-interpretable concepts [5658], and concept-guided relevance has recently been used as training signal to steer models away from spurious correlations in single fine-tuning stage, by explicitly suppressing background relevance [12]. C3L differs in both setting and mechanism: it targets continual learning, where explanations drift as the model is updated on sequence of tasks; it identifies the self-referential drift loop of pixel-level explanation-aware CL methods and replaces their model-derived targets with learner-independent concept targets; and rather than suppressing the background, it stabilizes its spatial structure with scale-invariant term, while background magnitude decreases through the crowding-out effect. Explanation-aware continual learning. Recognizing that catastrophic forgetting manifests as explanation drift alongside accuracy loss, Ebrahimi et al. [10] introduced RRR, which stores Grad3 CAM [42] saliency maps alongside replay exemplars and penalizes attention shift, demonstrating that models frequently preserve accuracy while fundamentally altering their decision process. Subsequent work extends this paradigm: Saha and Roy [13] propose saliency-guided exemplar packing to maximize buffer diversity, and Liu et al. [14] introduce task-adaptive saliency masks that adjust dynamically to forgetting patterns. While these methods show that explanation consistency provides valuable supervision beyond classification loss, they lead to self-referential drift loop. This drift loop is not merely an attribution noise issue - it is structural property of any scheme that derives targets from model-state-dependent saliency. The problem is compounded by well-documented brittleness of pixel-level attributions: they are notoriously noisy and prone to highlighting spurious correlations [59, 60], can be sensitive to imperceptible input perturbations [61] and may emphasize high-frequency texture artifacts rather than semantically meaningful object parts [11]. C3L breaks this loop, replacing model-state-dependent pixel targets with class-consistent, modelstate-independent concept-level supervision generated entirely offline before training. Concept discovery and visual grounding. Early concept-based models required extensive manual annotation [56, 17]. Label-free CBMs [15] use LLMs to generate concepts without supervision. SAM 3 [16] enables precise spatial localization of textual concepts. In this work, we do not aim to construct bottleneck model for inherent interpretability. Rather, we leverage these automated discovery and grounding pipelines as an offline pre-processing stage to synthesize rich, dense supervision signals. This allows us to anchor the models attention to semantic regions during continual learning, effectively replacing expensive manual concept annotation with scalable, crossinstance semantic consistent priors. Positioning. Prior region-level CL relies on model-state-dependent targets (e.g., CAM), creating self-referential drift loop we identify. C3L eliminates this loop via three axes no prior method addresses simultaneously: (1) target independence: offline generation prevents drift reinforcement; (2) semantic specificity: supervision targets are fine-grained attributes rather than coarse boundaries; and (3) cross-instance consistency: class-shared targets induce robust invariants. Finally, Table 13 isolates semantic specificity, confirming significant advantage over object-level masks using the identical SAM 3 model.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We present comprehensive empirical evaluation of C3L across diverse continual learning scenarios, model architectures, and evaluation protocols. Our experiments address four key research questions: (1) RQ1 (4.2): Does concept-level regularization reduce catastrophic forgetting more effectively than state-of-the-art methods? (2) RQ2 (4.3): Does C3L mitigate spurious correlations and explanation drift? (3) RQ3 (4.4): What are the contributions of C3Ls key components and design choices - dual regularization, buffer size, spatial grounding, explanation methods, task granularity, and concept discovery mechanism? (4) RQ4 (4.5): Can C3Ls training mechanism improve model robustness to out-of-distribution shifts (ImageNet-A and ObjectNet)? Success here suggests the model has internalized and generalized transferable semantic concepts rather than dataset-specific artifacts.

sections.title: 4.1 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. We evaluate on five benchmarks spanning fine-grained recognition and out-of-distribution generalization: CUB-200-2011 (CUB) [62] (200 bird species), DomainNet [63] (345 classes across 6 domains), ImageNet-R [64] (200 classes with artistic renditions), ImageNet-A [65] (200 classes with natural adversarial examples), ObjectNet [66] (113 classes with pose/background variations). These datasets represent both typical class-incremental benchmarks (CUB, DomainNet) and challenging 6 distribution shifts (ImageNet-R/A, ObjectNet) that test robustness beyond standard continual learning settings. Also, they exhibit significant domain gap with ImageNet (i.e., the pre-trained dataset). Following standard protocols [28, 5, 22], we split datasets into 10 sequential tasks (5 for DomainNet) with equal classes per task under class-incremental learning: task boundaries known during training but not at test, with classification over all encountered classes. For ObjectNet, 3 randomly sampled classes are excluded so that the remaining 110 classes divide evenly into tasks (Appendix B). Evaluation metrics. We report three standard continual learning metrics [4, 67]: (i) Average Accuracy (ACC) : the average accuracy on all the tasks after the last task has been learned, (ii) Average Forgetting (F) : mean accuracy drop on previous tasks, = 1 i=1 maxj{i,...,T } Ai,j Ai,T , where Ai,j is accuracy on task after training on task j, (iii) Average Incremental Accuracy (AIA) : mean accuracy after learning each task, capturing the models performance throughout the entire learning trajectory. For explanation evaluation (4.3), we measure: (i) Spurious Correlation Mitigation (Debiasing): following Lee et al. [68] and Bayasi et al. [69] we evaluate ACC over both Fitzpatrick17K (FITZ) [69] and Split ImageNet-100C (I-100C) [68] to evaluate the models reliance on spurious correlations. (ii) Semantic Localization: following Chefer et al. [44] we measure the mIoU, pixel accuracy (pixAcc), and mAP of the explanations on CUB. More details provided in Appendix H. (cid:80)T 1 Baselines. We compare against 20+ state-of-the-art methods spanning multiple paradigms. For CNNs: Regularization-based: EWC [6], LwF [70], PEC [21]; Replay-based: ER [71], iCaRL [4], DER++ [5], ER-ACE [18], CSReL-CL [19]; Explanation-aware: RRR [10], EPR [13] TASS [14]. For ViTs: Prompt-based: L2P [9], DualPrompt [22], CODA-Prompt [23]; General: SLCA [28], RanPAC [29]; Adapter-based: EASE [24], MOS [25], MIN [26], PLAN [27]. We also provide ViT-based implementation for RRR named RRR-ViT which uses Grad-CAM-ViT [44]. Joint Training is standard supervised fine-tuning on the i.i.d. union of all tasks data, without concept supervision; it is commonly regarded as an upper bound for continual learning methods that use the same supervision. Fine-Tuning is the naive sequential fine-tuning approach with the pre-trained model frozen. In this work, we focus on continual learning for widely used architectures such as CNNs and ViTs. While C3L could potentially be extended to concept bottleneck models (CBMs), systematically adapting CBMs to continual learning constitutes research problem in its own and is therefore left for future work. Controlled comparisons. To isolate the benefit of the choice of explanation method from C3L, we implement two controlled variants of RRR, called RRR-LRP and RRR-ViT-AttnLRP (for ResNet-18 and ViT-B respectively), that use our explanation methods instead of Grad-CAM. To isolate replay benefits, we add replay-augmented variants (-R) following Wang et al. [9]. All replay methods use identical buffer size (M = 1000) for fair comparison. Section 4.4 shows that C3L achieves competitive results against all baselines (with = 1000) using small buffer of size = 200. We follow original code-bases for implementation and hyperparameter settings to ensure the best possible performance. Implementation Details. We use ResNet-18 [72] (ImageNet-1K pretrained) and ViT-B/16 [73] (ImageNet-21K pretrained). C3L employs LRP [45] for CNNs and AttnLRP [47] for ViTs; all baselines use Grad-CAM [42] as unified evaluation protocol. Concept discovery follows Oikarinen et al. [15] with spatial grounding via SAM 3 [16]. Full configuration details are provided in Appendix B. Training Details. Regularization is applied exclusively to replay samples (M = 1000). Results are averaged over 5 runs (mean std), with statistical significance assessed via paired t-tests (p < 0.05). Full hyperparameter settings and training protocols are provided in Appendix B. C3L incurs an approximately 3% increase in training time relative to RRR (ResNet-18), due to explanation computation and regularization. This overhead is modest given the substantial performance improvements achieved. The method also requires only an additional 8% of storage compared to RRR. sections.title: 4.2 RQ1: Standard Continual Learning Performance
sections.content: Table 1 presents comprehensive results across ResNet-18 and ViT-B. Due to space constraints, the complete set of results, including all evaluated methods, is reported on Table 19 in the Appendix. C3L achieves consistent improvements in accuracy and forgetting across all datasets, outperforming state-of-the-art and explanation-based methods. Notably, Lconcept could also be applied to all training samples. However, we restrict it to replay examples to ensure fair comparison with prior replay methods. Results for this variant are reported in the full results table in the Appendix. critical question is whether gains stem from using superior explanation methods (LRP vs. GradCAM) rather than concept-level regularization. Our controlled comparisons provide clear evidence for the latter. RRR-ViT-AttnLRP (using AttnLRP instead of Grad-CAM) improves over RRR-ViT. However, C3L with AttnLRP achieves far greater gains. Since both use identical AttnLRP, this provides evidence for the benefit of concept-level over pixel-level regularization: semantically grounded regions provide substantially stronger supervision than raw saliency. The same pattern holds for ResNet-18. Replay-based methods mostly outperform other methods in both CNNs and ViTs. This aligns with recent findings [20] showing that replay-based methods benefit from preserving feature learning dynamics. We further observe that for ResNet-18, explanation-aware methods achieve very good performance, and are mostly better than regular replay-based methods. However, pixel-level methods may not distinguish between spurious correlations and semantic features. In contrast, C3L focuses on validated semantic concepts, providing cleaner supervision, which is also evident by the performance. This gap is further emphasized on Sec. 4.3. ViTs exhibit substantially lower forgetting than CNNs across all methods, likely reflecting the more stable representations of large-scale pretrained transformers. Notably, RRR-ViT sometimes outperforms prompt-based methods with replay (L2P-R, CODA-R), demonstrating that explanation consistency provides valuable regularization even for transformers. Nevertheless, C3L maintains consistent advantages across both architectures, demonstrating its effectiveness across distinct architectural families.

sections.title: 4.3 RQ2: Explanation Drift and Spurious Correlations
sections.content: Standard continual learning protocols do not assess whether methods mitigate spurious correlations or maintain focus on semantically meaningful features. To address this limitation, we adopt two complementary evaluation protocols: (1) Spurious Correlation Mitigation, measured by accuracy on FITZ and I100C, evaluating model reliance on spurious features (skin tone in FITZ and injected noise in I-100C); (2) Semantic Localization, evaluated using mIoU, pixAcc, and mAP of explanations on CUB annotated segments1, to quantify explanation drift. For (1), we follow prior work [69, 68] and 1https://data.caltech.edu/records/w9d68-gec53 8 fine-tune CNN model (ResNet-18 pretrained on ImageNet-1K). For (2), we evaluate the same CUBfinetuned model from Section 4.2. We compare C3L against representative baselines from Table 1 and Table 19. In addition, for protocol (1), we include two recent class-incremental learning methods for debiasing: BiasPruner (BP) [69] and BGS [68]. Further experimental and implementation details provided in Appendix H. As shown in Table 2, C3L consistently achieves the best performance across both accuracy and semantic localization metrics. The improvement in accuracy is consistent with our hypothesis that C3L anchors attention to semantically relevant features, thereby preventing the emergence of spurious correlations. Notably, C3L outperforms specialized debiasing methods on accuracy across both datasets. In contrast, pixel-level explanation-aware baselines (RRR, EPR) and other continual learning methods (L2P, MOS, MIN) show lower semantic localization scores and spurious correlation mitigation performance. These results show that concept-grounded regularization systematically redirects model attention from irrelevant cues to semantically meaningful features, thereby mitigating explanation drift, improving the quality of model reasoning, and limiting the accumulation of spurious correlations. sections.title: 4.5 RQ4: Robustness to Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Samples
sections.content: We evaluate robustness to OOD samples using setup inspired by [74], which studies feature transferability by training on subset of ImageNet classes. Specifically, we construct compact fine-tuning dataset for C3L by randomly selecting 5 images per class from half of the ImageNet1K [75] categories, resulting in total of 2,500 training images. This sparse sampling is motivated by computational considerations and serves to assess data efficiency under limited supervision, while random class selection ensures broad semantic coverage. Experiments are conducted using ResNet-18 and ViT-B models pretrained on ImageNet-1K. Robustness is evaluated specifically on ImageNet-A and ObjectNet (restricted to classes overlapping ImageNet-1K) as these benchmarks contain challenging samples that commonly cause failures in ImageNet-pretrained models. Further details are provided in the Appendix. Table 5 details the classification accuracy before and after finetuning with C3L in comparison with RRR (RRR-ViT). We observe significant increase in accuracy when employing C3Ls semantic-based regularization. In contrast, RRR yields only negligible gains (and sometimes even decrease the accuracy), highlighting its lower robustness capabilities in this setting. This isolates the impact of semantic features, demonstrating their substantial capacity to modulate model behavior. Full experiments, including EPR and TASS, along segmentation evaluation are provided in the Appendix.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented C3L, framework that breaks the self-referential drift loop and mitigates explanation drift by anchoring representations to semantically grounded concepts. By regularizing attention toward semantic attributes rather than unstable pixel-level saliency, C3L promotes learning of transferable features that better resist spurious correlations and explanation drifts. Our automated framework eliminates the need for manual annotation, making concept-based supervision scalable for continual learning. Extensive evaluation across five benchmarks demonstrates that C3L establishes state-of-the-art performance in continual learning, particularly under challenging out-of-distribution shifts. Limitations and future work are detailed in the Appendix.

sections.title: B Implementation Details
sections.content: Full Implementation Details. We use ResNet-18 [72] (ImageNet-1K pretrained) for CNN experiments and ViT-B/16 (ViT-B) [73] (ImageNet-21K pretrained) for transformer experiments. For explanation generation, we employ LRP [45] with ϵ-rule (ϵ = 106) for CNNs and AttnLRP [47] for ViTs. For saliency map evaluation (e.g., Tab. 2), explanations for all baselines are generated post-training using Grad-CAM [42] for CNNs and Grad-CAM-ViT [44] for ViTs. While C3L yields marginally higher scores when evaluated on its native LRP maps, we report Grad-CAM results to maintain unified evaluation protocol. C3Ls saliency maps are min-max normalized to [0, 1] prior to BCE computation. Concept discovery follows the approach from Oikarinen et al. [15] which resulting in concept set per class, filtered by occurrence rate (νocc 0.15) and coverage (νcov 0.2). Spatial grounding uses SAM 3 [16] with confidence threshold τconf = 0.3. We validate these configuration choices in Appendix F. Full Training Details. We apply regularization only to replay samples, as current task samples lack reference explanations. The replay buffer (size = 1000) is populated via uniform random sampling from previous tasks. Hyperparameters: λconcept = 1.0, λstab = 1.5 for CNNs, and λconcept = 0.8, λstab = 1.2 for ViTs. These values were selected based on validation set performance (validated in the Appendix). Results are averaged over 5 runs with different random seeds and task orderings. We report mean standard deviation and assess statistical significance (p < 0.05) using paired t-tests comparing C3L against the best-performing baseline in each experimental setting. Training Protocols. For our method, we employ stochastic gradient descent (SGD) for both model architectures, using batch size of 128 and learning rate of 0.001. Training is conducted for 20 epochs on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, ObjectNet, and DomainNet, and for 50 epochs on the CUB dataset. All baselines were used according to the recommended setup reported in their papers and code. Task Splits. All datasets are split into tasks with an equal number of classes per task: CUB (200 classes), ImageNet-R (200), and ImageNet-A (200) into 10 tasks of 20 classes, and DomainNet (345 classes) into 5 tasks of 69 classes. ObjectNet contains 113 classes that overlap with ImageNet-1K, which cannot be divided evenly into 10 tasks; we therefore randomly exclude 3 classes and split the remaining 110 classes into 10 tasks of 11 classes each. All methods use the same class subset and splits. 16 Concept Discovery. We used the implementation from [15] with GPT-4o-mini [76] and used the prompts from the original github repository 2 without the "around" prompts. Spatial Grounding Parameters. For SAM 3 segmentation, we use confidence threshold τconf = 0.3 and used the Ultralytics implementation 3. Lower thresholds increase false positives (irrelevant regions), while higher thresholds miss valid concept instances. We validate this choice in Appendix F.7. Replay Buffer. The replay buffer size is set to = 1000 for fair comparison with baselines. We use uniform random sampling across previous tasks to populate the buffer. Each task contributes equally to maintain balanced representation. Computational Environment. All experiments are conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs using PyTorch. For both ResNet-18 and ViT-B experiments, we use single-GPU training.

sections.title: D Method Design Justification
sections.content: D.1 Background Regularization Strategy central design choice in C3L is how to regularize non-concept (background) regions. Unlike pixel-level alignment methods that indiscriminately anchor explanations to reference saliency map, C3L introduces semantic prior that explicitly reallocates relevance toward intrinsic class attributes while constraining background behavior. Rationale. Our design is motivated by three considerations. First, mitigating spurious correlations: by enforcing full relevance within discovered concept regions, we can leverage the finite nature of the relevance budget. While relevance conservation is approximate in modern deep networks [46], empirically, maximizing relevance on foreground concepts encourages redistribution of mass away from the background. This crowding-out effect helps suppress spurious cues without requiring explicit penalization. Second, incomplete concept discovery: automated concept generation may omit valid diagnostic features (e.g., fine-grained parts). Explicit background suppression risks eliminating such implicitly learned cues present in the pretrained model. Third, context preservation: background regions encode stable contextual information (e.g., pose, geometry, scale) learned during pretraining, which can support generalization and should not be erased. To balance these factors, Lstab enforces stability, preserving the spatial structure of background relevance, rather than suppression. While the relative magnitude of background relevance naturally decreases due to relevance reallocation, anchoring its pattern prevents drift toward new, task-specific artifacts. Empirical Support. We compare three strategies: (i) the full C3L, (ii) no background regularization (w/o Lstab on Section 4.4), and (iii) explicit background suppression without replay (C3L-NoReplay on Section F.1). Experiments with ViT-B on ImageNet-R and CUB  (Table 8)  show that stabilization outperforms both alternatives; since (iii) also removes replay, the comparison with (ii) is the one that isolates the background term, confirming that preserving pretrained contextual priors while preventing spurious correlations yields the best trade-off. Quantitative Evidence for the Crowding-Out Effect In Section 3.3, we introduced the concept of relevance reallocation as mechanism by which enforcing high attribution within concept regions indirectly suppresses spurious background correlations. This phenomenon, which we term the crowding-out effect, operates through the approximate conservation of relevance mass in neural networks [46]. Specifically, when the model is encouraged to concentrate relevance within semantically meaningful concept regions via Lconcept, the finite relevance budget naturally reallocates away from non-diagnostic background regions, even without explicit suppression. While Section D.1 provided empirical evidence via ablation studies, critical question remains: does relevance mass actually move from background to concept regions during training, or do both regions 18 Table 9: Relevance mass flow analysis across training tasks on CUB T1 test set. Results demonstrate reallocation of relevance from background to concept regions, validating the crowding-out mechanism.

This shift occurs despite the model learning 180 new classes across subsequent tasks, which typically induces explanation drift toward spurious features [10]. The 0.20 gain in 19 concept share is therefore matched by 0.18 reduction in background share: relevance is reallocated from background to concept regions rather than added on top of it, consistent with the crowding-out effect described in Section 3.3. These results validate the theoretical mechanism proposed in Section 3.3: by enforcing high relevance within concept regions through Lconcept, the model satisfies this constraint by reallocating relevance mass away from background regions. The background stabilization term Lstab prevents drift to new spurious artifacts while allowing this magnitude reduction. Together, the dual regularization creates crowding-out effect where semantically grounded concepts compete for and capture an increasing share of the relevance budget, naturally suppressing background correlations without explicit penalization. This analysis provides the first direct quantitative evidence for the crowding-out effect in conceptbased continual learning. Unlike previous work that measures only final explanation quality [10, 13], tracking relevance flow throughout training reveals the mechanism by which concept regularization mitigates catastrophic forgetting. The reallocation of relevance from backgrounds to concepts demonstrates that semantic anchoring actively reshapes the models decision-making process, not merely preserving existing attention patterns. Importantly, this redistribution occurs without explicit background suppression. The crowdingout effect emerges naturally from the interaction between concept overlap enforcement (Lconcept), background stability (Lstab), and approximate relevance conservation. This validates our design choice in favor of stability over suppression (Appendix D.1): while background relevance magnitude decreases due to crowding-out, its spatial pattern remains anchored to pretrained priors, preserving useful contextual information while preventing spurious correlations.

In contrast, concept-level masks emphasize discriminative attributes, resulting in denser and more localized supervision that more effectively constrains model attention. Additionally, object-level segmentations often encompass redundant or weakly informative regions, for example, assigning high importance to the entire body of Brown Bear, whereas concept-level supervision can focus on minimal yet sufficient subset of salient parts. [44], on the CUB dataset, which provides ground-truth segmentation annotations4. Datasets. Split ImageNet-100C (I-100C) [68] is derived from Split ImageNet-100, which consists of 10 sequential tasks, each containing 10 disjoint classes randomly sampled from ImageNet-1K. To introduce controlled spurious correlations, we inject Gaussian noise disproportionately: (α 100)% of the samples from one randomly selected class are corrupted, while only 1% of samples from the remaining classes are affected, for skew ratio α 0.01. We consider seven bias levels by varying the skew ratio. Fitzpatrick17k (FITZ) [80] is large-scale clinical dermatology dataset comprising 16,577 images across 114 skin conditions, each annotated with Fitzpatrick Skin Type (FST) on six-point scale. Due to its pronounced skin-tone imbalance-approximately 47% of images correspond to FST III and only about 13% to FST VVI-the dataset is widely used to evaluate robustness and bias mitigation under real-world demographic skew. Training Configuration. We employ the ResNet-18 and ViT-B backbones pre-trained on ImageNet1K and ImageNet-21k respectively. For spurious correlation mitigation, we finetune ResNet-18 on both FITZ and I-100C using the exact same setup reported in the original codebase of every baseline. Specifically, for BGS, we used its best performing configuration on the accuracy metric reported in the paper, which is DER+BGS. For semantic localization, both models are fine-tuned on the CUB using the same protocol from the main paper. Semantic Localization Evaluation. Here, our goal is to asses the quality of semantic localization and explanation map consistency. We evaluate explanation quality using the CUB dataset, which provides ground-truth object segmentation masks. Following Chefer et al. [44], we threshold saliency maps at the 50th percentile to produce binary masks and compute: (1) mIoU: Mean Intersectionover-Union between explanation masks and ground-truth objects, (2) pixAcc: Pixel-wise accuracy (correctly classified pixels / total pixels), and (3) mAP: Mean Average Precision across IoU thresholds [0.5, 0.55, . . . , 0.95]. Higher values indicate that explanations better localize semantic object regions 4https://data.caltech.edu/records/w9d68-gec53 25 rather than spurious backgrounds. Since C3L is trained to align relevance with concept regions on the object, improved localization is partly expected by design; the spurious-correlation results on FITZ and I-100C provide complementary evidence that does not rely on segmentation. H.2 Robustness Tests Further Details OOD Evaluation Protocol. Our setup is inspired by [74], which studies feature transferability by training on subset of ImageNet classes; here, we fine-tune on class subset and evaluate on OOD benchmarks. Dataset Construction. We curate lightweight dataset by sampling 5 images from 500 randomly selected ImageNet-1K [75] classes resulting with 2,500 samples. This ensures broad semantic coverage while rigorously testing data efficiency under limited supervision. Models and Benchmarks. We utilize ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18 and ViT-B models. Testing is performed on ImageNet-A and ObjectNet (restricted to overlapping classes), which represent challenging OOD shifts that ImageNet-pretrained models mostly fail with. Performance is measured using classification accuracy (%) and mean Intersection over Union (mIoU). For mIoU, we compare the explanation maps, computed as in Tab. 2, against object segmentations generated by prompting SAM 3 with the ground-truth class labels. Training. We execute the complete C3L framework-comprising concept discovery, validation, and grounding - on the 2,500-sample subset. First, we perform automatic concept generation [15] for the 500 selected classes. We then validate these candidate concepts using 40 images per class, yielding filtered concept set for each category. Subsequently, we ground these concepts for every sample in the training subset by prompting SAM 3 with the filtered concepts (one prompt per concept), thereby generating concept maps. Additionally, we employ LRP and AttnLRP to produce explanations for each image. Finally, the models are fine-tuned exclusively on this subset using the C3L approach, leveraging the derived concept maps and explanations as supervision. For both RRR and RRR-ViT we used the same setup reported by the authors [10] for the fine-tuning phase. Full results. We additionally evaluate EPR and TASS, including their ViT-adapted variants (EPRViT, TASS-ViT), to enable comprehensive comparison with explanation-aware baselines. The ViT adaptations follow standard practice, using Grad-CAM for ViTs [44] and generating explanations from the [CLS] token, as commonly adopted in prior work. The results mirror the trends observed in the main paper: C3L consistently outperforms all explanation-aware methods in robustness to out-of-distribution data. sections.content: I.1 Performance without Foundation Models Usage To disentangle the semantic guidance and foundation models factors, we remove foundation models from the training pipeline and instead conduct experiments on the PartImageNet dataset [81], which provides ground-truth part-level annotations. Although part annotations are not equivalent to semantic concepts, this setting offers controlled evaluation that isolates the effect of semantic guidance. The results therefore illustrate the benefits of leveraging semantic features for continual learning independently of foundation models. While we aim to ensure fair comparison with existing baselines, we note that equipping those methods with the same foundation-model guidance used in our approach would be conceptually similar to applying our method or to the experimental setting presented in Table 13. Experimental Setup. We evaluate ResNet-18 trained from scratch on class-incremental split of PartImageNet. We used 150 classes (out of 158, removing 8 randomly sampled classes) partitioned into 10 tasks of 15 classes each. Baselines: Standard ER [71], DER++ [5], RRR [10], EPR [13], and our original C3L. C3L-PG (Part-Guided): Instead of using GPT-4o-mini or SAM 3, we used the datasets ground-truth part masks as the semantic concepts for our dual regularization objective. Results and Discussion. I.2 Isolating SAM 3s Inherent Capabilities from C3Ls Gains natural concern is whether C3Ls performance gains stem primarily from the rich visual knowledge already encoded in SAM 3, rather than from the proposed concept-guided continual learning framework itself. To address this, we evaluate SAM 3 as standalone zero-shot classifier, entirely bypassing the C3L training pipeline, and compare its best achievable accuracy against C3L trained under the standard continual learning protocol. Experimental Setup. We construct two zero-shot classification variants that maximally exploit SAM 3s pretrained grounding capabilities, without any continual learning. Variant 1 (category name prompt): For each test image, we prompt SAM 3 with the class category name (e.g., American Robin) and assign the label corresponding to the concept mask with the highest confidence score returned by SAM 3. Variant 2 (attribute prompt): For each test image, we prompt SAM 3 with the full set of filtered concept attributes for every candidate class (e.g., red breast, dark cap, yellow beak) and assign the label corresponding to the class whose concept set achieves the highest joint detection confidence across its attributes. 27 Both variants use the same filtered concept sets and the same SAM 3 configuration (τconf = 0.3) as C3L, and are evaluated on CUB and ImageNet-R. This indicates that SAM 3s grounding capabilities alone do not account for the performance of C3L. Interpretation and scope of comparison. We note an important protocol difference: zero-shot evaluation and class-incremental continual learning are not directly comparable tasks. Zero-shot classification presents all classes simultaneously without any sequential training or forgetting dynamics, which is precisely the challenge that C3L is designed to address. We view this experiment as complementary to the controlled ablations presented in Table 13 (same SAM 3 model, concept-level versus object-level prompts) and Table 21 (concept-guided learning without any vision-language model). Together, these three experiments isolate the contribution of C3Ls framework along distinct axes: foundation model versus no foundation model, concept-level versus coarser supervision, and continual learning versus zero-shot classification. I.3 Semantic Depth Over Object Segmentation We examined the impact of mask granularity in Appendix  (Table 13)  to further emphasize the contribution of our semantic anchoring approach. We implemented baseline using the exact same SAM 3 foundation model but prompted it for object-level segmentation (masking the entire object) rather than our fine-grained concept-level segmentation (masking specific attributes like beak or wing). The results demonstrate that concept-level supervision yields superior performance compared to object-level masks. This suggests that semantic guidance is also driver of our results, rather than merely the presence of foundationmodel-derived segmentation masks. I.4 Foundation Models as Automated Annotators Our framework utilizes GPT-4o-mini and SAM 3 to automate the generation of semantic supervision. We leverage these foundation models in an offline preprocessing stage to decompose images into semantic regions. We view this process as automated annotation leveraging foundation model priors, distinct from knowledge distillation in that we do not transfer class predictions or latent representations. Importantly, this automated concept discovery and grounding stage is as an offline pre-processing stage. In standard knowledge distillation, student model is typically trained to mimic the soft targets (logits) or align with the latent feature space of teacher model. In contrast, C3L does not access the class probability distributions or internal embeddings of the foundation models. Instead, these models function as an automated framework to generate binary spatial masks (Mconcept). These masks provide the "where" (spatial attention targets), but the model must autonomously learn the "what" (discriminative features) from the training data labels. This allows us to inject human-interpretable priors without leaking instance-specific predictive information.

sections.title: J Computational Analysis
sections.content: We analyze the computational costs of C3L to provide practical guidance for deployment. For clarity, we compare C3L primarily against RRR, which allows us to more directly highlight the computational trade-offs introduced by concept-level regularization. For this analysis, we used the ImageNet-R dataset to provide specific details. Training overhead. The additional computational cost of C3L relative to RRR arises from two main factors: (i) the computation of LRP-based explanations instead of Grad-CAM, and (ii) the evaluation of the two regularization terms (Eqs. 35). Across both ResNet-18 and ViT-B architectures, the resulting training times remain comparable to those of RRR, with only minor increases in wall-clock time. Specifically, when training ResNet-18 on ImageNet-R, C3L incurs 3% increase in end-to-end training time (from 28 min to 29 min). For ViT-B, the corresponding overhead is 6% (from 1.5 to 1.6 h). These results indicate that the additional training cost introduced by C3L is modest relative to the performance gains it achieves. Preprocessing costs. C3L incurs small additional replay preprocessing costs. Specifically, concept generation using GPT-4o-mini requires approximately 15 minutes for 200 classes, while spatial grounding with SAM 3 on 1,000 replay samples takes 18 minutes on single A100 GPU. In addition, validating the generated concepts over the sample set requires approximately 25 minutes (but optional), and computing LRP-based saliency maps for the replay set adds further 5 minutes. This results in total of 63 minutes (38 without concept validation). Memory footprint. In addition to the standard replay buffer (86 MB for 1,000 samples at 224 224 resolution), C3L stores binary concept masks (12 MB) and reference saliency maps (23 MB). By comparison, RRR requires the same replay buffer and 26 MB to store Grad-CAM saliency maps. Consequently, the incremental memory overhead of C3L arises primarily from storing concept masks, corresponding to an approximately 8% increase in memory usage, which is negligible in modern systems. Practical deployment considerations. For streaming scenarios where low latency is critical, preprocessing can be performed asynchronously during task transitions or offloaded to separate infrastructure. Alternatively, Table 4 demonstrates that C3L achieves competitive performance with = 200 (reducing preprocessing significantly) while still outperforming baselines using = 1000. For resource-constrained settings, our replay-free variant (C3L-NoReplay, Table 10) eliminates replay preprocessing entirely while surpassing standard ER, demonstrating that semantic regularization provides value even without this large preprocessing phase.

sections.title: L Failure Cases
sections.content: L.1 Concept Discovery Failures While automated concept discovery achieves quite high retention rate, some generated concepts fail filtering: Too Abstract. Concepts like graceful posture", aggressive demeanor", or "natural habitat" describe semantic properties but lack clear visual grounding. SAM 3 cannot reliably localize such concepts, leading to noisy masks. 29 Figure 3: Qualitative comparison of explanation maps produced by C3L and baseline methods before and after continual learning. Explanation maps produced using ViT-B w.r.t. the classes (top to bottom): lorikeet, usb cable, common newt, Triturus vulgaris, and accordion, piano accordion. Too Rare. Concepts appearing in < 15% of class instances (e.g., open beak" for birds, raised paw" for dogs) fail occurrence rate criteria. While visually grounded when present, their rarity makes them unsuitable for class-wide regularization. Ambiguous. Concepts like medium size" or dark color" lack clear spatial boundaries. For instance, SAM 3 may produce inconsistent masks for "dark color" depending on lighting. L.2 Segmentation Failures SAM 3 rarely produces noisy or incorrect masks: Small or Occluded Features. Fine-grained concepts covering < 2% of image area (e.g., eye-ring" on small birds, toe claws" on animals) are missed or segmented with low IoU. This primarily affects fine-grained datasets like CUB. Concept Ambiguity. Polysemous concepts (e.g., fluffy texture" can describe fur, clouds, or cotton) may segment unintended regions. While validation filters some cases, occasional false positives remain.

sections.title: M Limitations and Future Work
sections.content: Limitations. While C3L advances continual learning through semantic grounding, several limitations warrant consideration. First, our approach relies on foundation models for automated concept generation. Although such models are increasingly used to guide learning in related domains [8284] and have driven recent breakthroughs in many, they may also introduce failure modes. For instance, spatial grounding may fail if language models produce non-visual or ambiguous concepts. We mitigate this through occurrence rate and coverage validation, but more sophisticated concept quality metrics could improve robustness. Second, C3L adds computational overhead for the concept and explanation map preprocessing procedure. Yet, this cost is modest relative to the performance gains. Third, our evaluation focuses on vision tasks. Extending concept-based regularization to other modalities (language, audio, multimodal) requires domain-specific concept discovery mechanisms. Fourth, the reference saliency used by Lstab is model-derived: while its magnitude is free to decay under crowding-out, the relative spatial pattern of background relevance at buffer insertion is preserved, so spurious background cues already present at that point are attenuated rather than fully removed. 30 Broader impact. Beyond technical contributions, our work has important implications for deploying continual learning systems in safety-critical domains. By maintaining interpretable reasoning patterns alongside predictive accuracy, C3L enables practitioners to monitor whether models learn reliably or develop hidden vulnerabilities through spurious correlations. This transparency is crucial for applications like medical diagnosis, autonomous systems, and content moderation where understanding how decisions are made is as important as ensuring they are correct. Moreover, our automated framework demonstrates that semantic grounding need not require extensive human supervision, making interpretable continual learning more accessible to practitioners without domain expertise in explainable AI. Future directions. This work opens several promising avenues for future research. First, extending concept-level regularization to domain-incremental and task-free (online) continual learning settings may better address scenarios with gradually shifting input distributions or unknown task boundaries. Second, exploring concept compositionality, namely, whether concepts learned for one class can be reused or recombined for related classes in subsequent tasks, could enable more efficient and scalable knowledge accumulation. Third, integrating concept-based regularization with parameter-efficient adaptation techniques for large visionlanguage models may combine the benefits of semantic grounding with efficient fine-tuning. Fourth, developing theoretical frameworks that characterize when and why concept-level regularization outperforms pixel-level approaches would provide principled guidance for the design of explanation-aware continual learning methods. Additionally, leveraging around prompts [15] to selectively preserve informative background regions, rather than suppressing all background content, may further reduce reliance on spurious correlations. Investigating whether concept-level regularization can support the detection of distribution shifts, by monitoring changes in concept activation patterns, could enable adaptive systems that identify novel contexts and trigger human intervention when needed. Finally, we believe that extending this approach to knowledge distillation presents promising direction; in scenarios where teacher model relies heavily on spurious correlations, concept-guided regularization could actively intervene during distillation, allowing the student to extract valuable predictive knowledge while strictly suppressing the inheritance of the teachers flawed reasoning patterns.
